verses.zh: 我们坚固的人应该担代不坚固人的软弱，不求自己的喜悦。
verses.en: But we who are strong ought to bear with the failings of the weak, and not just please ourselves.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “and not please ourselves.” NT Greek negatives used in contrast like this are often not absolute, but relative: “not so much one as the other.”

verses.zh: 我们各人务要叫邻舍喜悦，使他得益处，建立德行。
verses.en: Let each of us please his neighbor for his good to build him up.

verses.zh: 因为基督也不求自己的喜悦，如经上所记：「辱骂你人的辱骂都落在我身上。」
verses.en: For even Christ did not please himself, but just as it is written, “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Ps 69:9.

verses.zh: 从前所写的圣经都是为教训我们写的，叫我们因圣经所生的忍耐和安慰可以得着盼望。
verses.en: For everything that was written in former times was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and through encouragement of the scriptures we may have hope.

verses.zh: 但愿赐忍耐安慰的　神叫你们彼此同心，效法基督耶稣，
verses.en: Now may the God of endurance and comfort give you unity with one another[NOTE:1] in accordance with Christ Jesus,
notes: Grk “grant you to think the same among one another.”

verses.zh: 一心一口荣耀　神―我们主耶稣基督的父！
verses.en: so that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

verses.zh: 所以，你们要彼此接纳，如同基督接纳你们一样，使荣耀归与　神。
verses.en: Receive one another, then, just as Christ also received you, to God’s glory.

verses.zh: 我说，基督是为　神真理作了受割礼人的执事，要证实所应许列祖的话，
verses.en: For I tell you that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised[NOTE:1] on behalf of God’s truth to confirm the promises made to the fathers,[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “of the circumcision”; that is, the Jews.
Or “to the patriarchs.”

verses.zh: 并叫外邦人因他的怜悯荣耀　神。如经上所记：因此，我要在外邦中称赞你，歌颂你的名；
verses.en: and thus the Gentiles glorify God for his mercy.[NOTE:1] As it is written, “Because of this I will confess you among the Gentiles, and I will sing praises to your name.”[NOTE:2]
notes: There are two major syntactical alternatives which are both awkward: (1) One could make “glorify” dependent on “Christ has become a minister” and coordinate with “to confirm” and the result would be rendered “Christ has become a minister of circumcision to confirm the promises…and so that the Gentiles might glorify God.” (2) One could make “glorify” dependent on “I tell you” and coordinate with “Christ has become a minister” and the result would be rendered “I tell you that Christ has become a minister of circumcision…and that the Gentiles glorify God.” The second rendering is preferred.
A quotation from Ps 18:49.

verses.zh: 又说：你们外邦人当与主的百姓一同欢乐；
verses.en: And again it says: “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.”[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Deut 32:43.

verses.zh: 又说：外邦啊，你们当赞美主！万民哪，你们都当颂赞他！
verses.en: And again, “Praise the Lord all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples praise him.”[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Ps 117:1.

verses.zh: 又有以赛亚说：将来有耶西的根，就是那兴起来要治理外邦的；外邦人要仰望他。
verses.en: And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, and the one who rises to rule over the Gentiles, in him will the Gentiles hope.”[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Isa 11:10.

verses.zh: 但愿使人有盼望的　神，因信将诸般的喜乐、平安充满你们的心，使你们藉着圣灵的能力大有盼望！
verses.en: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in him,[NOTE:1] so that you may abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
notes: Grk “in the believing” or “as [you] believe,” with the object “him” supplied from the context. The referent could be God (15:13a) or Christ (15:12).

verses.zh: 弟兄们，我自己也深信你们是满有良善，充足了诸般的知识，也能彼此劝戒。
verses.en: But I myself am fully convinced about you, my brothers and sisters,[NOTE:1] that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able to instruct one another.
notes: Grk “brothers.” See note on the phrase “brothers and sisters” in 1:13.

verses.zh: 但我稍微放胆写信给你们，是要提醒你们的记性，特因　神所给我的恩典，
verses.en: But I have written more boldly to you on some points so as to remind you, because of the grace given to me by God

verses.zh: 使我为外邦人作基督耶稣的仆役，作　神福音的祭司，叫所献上的外邦人，因着圣灵成为圣洁，可蒙悦纳。
verses.en: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. I serve[NOTE:1] the gospel of God[NOTE:2] like a priest, so that the Gentiles may become an acceptable offering,[NOTE:3] sanctified by the Holy Spirit.
notes: Grk “serving.” This is a continuation of the previous sentence in the Greek text, but in keeping with contemporary English style, a new sentence was started here in the translation.

The genitive in the phrase τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ θεοῦ (to euangelion tou theou, “the gospel of God”) could be translated as either a subjective genitive (“the gospel which God brings”) or an objective genitive (“the gospel about God”). Either is grammatically possible. This is possibly an instance of a plenary genitive (see ExSyn 119-21; M. Zerwick, Biblical Greek, §§36-39). If so, an interplay between the two concepts is intended: The gospel which God brings is in fact the gospel about himself.

Grk “so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable.” This could be understood to refer to an offering belonging to the Gentiles (a possessive genitive) or made by the Gentiles (subjective genitive), but more likely the phrase should be understood as an appositive genitive, with the Gentiles themselves consisting of the offering (so J. D. G. Dunn, Romans [WBC 38], 2:860). The latter view is reflected in the translation “so that the Gentiles may become an acceptable offering.”

verses.zh: 所以论到　神的事，我在基督耶稣里有可夸的。
verses.en: So I boast[NOTE:1] in Christ Jesus about the things that pertain to God.
notes: ‡ After οὖν (oun), several significant Alexandrian and Western mss (B C D F G 81 365) have τήν (tēn). The article is lacking in א A Ψ 33 1175 1241 1505 1739 1881 M however. P46 supplies a relative pronoun and has a different reading entirely (“which I have [as a] boast”). Articles were frequently introduced to clarify the meaning of the text. In this instance, since the word modified (καύχησιν, kauchēsin) is third declension, a visual oversight (resulting in omission) is less likely. Hence, the shorter reading is probably earlier. The difference in translation between these first two options is negligible (“I have the boast” or “I have a boast”). NA28 puts the article in brackets, indicating some doubt as to its authenticity.tn Grk “Therefore I have a boast.”

verses.zh: 除了基督藉我做的那些事，我甚么都不敢提，只提他藉我言语作为，用神迹奇事的能力，并圣灵的能力，使外邦人顺服；
verses.en: For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me in order to bring about the obedience[NOTE:1] of the Gentiles, by word and deed,
notes: Grk “unto obedience.”

verses.zh: 甚至我从耶路撒冷，直转到以利哩古，到处传了基督的福音。
verses.en: in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Spirit of God. So from Jerusalem even as far as Illyricum I have fully preached the gospel of Christ.

verses.zh: 我立了志向，不在基督的名被称过的地方传福音，免得建造在别人的根基上。
verses.en: And in this way I desire to preach where Christ has not been named, so as not to build on another person’s foundation,

verses.zh: 就如经上所记：未曾闻知他信息的，将要看见；未曾听过的，将要明白。
verses.en: but as it is written: “Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Isa 52:15.

verses.zh: 我因多次被拦阻，总不得到你们那里去。
verses.en: This is the reason I was often hindered from coming to you.

verses.zh: 但如今，在这里再没有可传的地方，而且这好几年，我切心想望到西班牙去的时候，可以到你们那里，
verses.en: But now there is nothing more to keep me[NOTE:1] in these regions, and I have for many years desired[NOTE:2] to come to you
notes: Grk “now no longer having a place…I have.”
Grk “but having a desire…for many years.”

verses.zh: 盼望从你们那里经过，得见你们，先与你们彼此交往，心里稍微满足，然后蒙你们送行。
verses.en: when I go to Spain. For I hope to visit you when I pass through and that you will help me[NOTE:1] on my journey there, after I have enjoyed your company for a while.
notes: Grk “and to be helped by you.” The passive construction was changed to an active one in the translation.

verses.zh: 但现在，我往耶路撒冷去供给圣徒。
verses.en: But now I go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints.

verses.zh: 因为马其顿和亚该亚人乐意凑出捐项给耶路撒冷圣徒中的穷人。
verses.en: For Macedonia and Achaia are pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem.

verses.zh: 这固然是他们乐意的，其实也算是所欠的债；因外邦人既然在他们属灵的好处上有分，就当把养身之物供给他们。
verses.en: For they were pleased to do this, and indeed they are indebted to the Jerusalem saints.[NOTE:1] For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they are obligated also to minister to them in material things.
notes: Grk “to them”; the referent (the Jerusalem saints) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 等我办完了这事，把这善果向他们交付明白，我就要路过你们那里，往西班牙去。
verses.en: Therefore after I have completed this and have safely delivered this bounty to them,[NOTE:1] I will set out for Spain by way of you,
notes: Grk “have sealed this fruit to them.”

verses.zh: 我也晓得，去的时候必带着基督丰盛的恩典而去。
verses.en: and I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of Christ’s blessing.

verses.zh: 弟兄们，我藉着我们主耶稣基督，又藉着圣灵的爱，劝你们与我一同竭力，为我祈求　神，
verses.en: Now I urge you, brothers and sisters,[NOTE:1] through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to join fervently with me in prayer to God on my behalf.
notes: Grk “brothers.” See note on the phrase “brothers and sisters” in 1:13.

verses.zh: 叫我脱离在犹太不顺从的人，也叫我为耶路撒冷所办的捐项可蒙圣徒悦纳，
verses.en: Pray[NOTE:1] that I may be rescued from those who are disobedient in Judea and that my ministry in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
notes: Verses 30-31 form one long sentence in the Greek but have been divided into two distinct sentences for clarity in English.

verses.zh: 并叫我顺着　神的旨意，欢欢喜喜地到你们那里，与你们同得安息。
verses.en: so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company.

verses.zh: 愿赐平安的　神常和你们众人同在。阿们！
verses.en: Now may the God of peace be with all of you. Amen.[NOTE:1]
notes: Some mss lack the word “Amen” here, one of them (P46) also inserting 16:25-27 at this point. See the note at 16:25 for more information.

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ROMANS 15:1-13

- The discussion about Christian freedom and responsibility is continuing in Rom. 15:1-13 (or at
least Rom. 15:6) from Romans 14. Remember, chapter divisions are not inspired.

- The entire argument of Rom. 14:1-15:13 could be outlined as

- accept one another because God accepts us in Christ (cf. Rom. 14:1,3; 15:7)

- do not judge one another because Christ is our only Master and Judge (cf. Rom. 14:3-12)

- love is more important than personal freedom (cf. Rom. 14:13-23)

- follow Christ's example and lay down your rights for others' edification and good (cf.
Rom. 15:1-13)

- Romans 15:5-6 reflects the three-fold purpose of the entire context of Rom. 14:1-15:13

- live in harmony with one another

- live in accordance with Christ's example

- with unified hearts and lips offer united praise to God

- This same tension between personal freedom and corporate responsibility is dealt with in
1 Corinthians 8-10 and Colossians 2:16-23.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ROMANS 15:1-6

1Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those without strength and not just please ourselves. 2Each of us is to please his neighbor for his good, to his edification. 3For even Christ did not please Himself; but as it is written, " The reproaches of those who reproached You fell on Me." 4For whatever was written in earlier times was written for our instruction, so that through perseverance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. 5Now may the God who gives perseverance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus, 6so that with one accord you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

15:1

NASB
"Now we who are strong ought to bear the weakness

of those without strength"

NKJV
"We then who are strong ought to bear with the

scruples of the weak"

NRSV
"We who are strong ought to put up with the failing of the weak"

TEV
"We who are strong in the faith ought to help

the weak to carry their burdens"

NJB
"We who are strong have a duty to put up with

the qualms of the weak"

REB
"Those of us who are strong must accept as our burden

the tender scruples of the weak"

Peshitta
"We then who are strong ought to bear the weakness of the weak"

These are two PRESENT INFINITIVES used in the sense of IMPERATIVES.
The mentioning of "the strong" and "weak" shows that Romans 15 continues the discussion begun in Rom. 14:1. It seems
to reflect the tension within the Roman Church, and all churches, on the way Christians live their lives in

- biblically ambiguous areas

- OT requirements

- reactions to non-moral, cultural issues

A good book that has been very helpful to me in this area is Gordon Fee, Gospel and Spirit.

For modern English readers, to label the two perspectives "strong" and "weak" is to prejudice the
groups. This was not Paul's intent. The strong group referred to those who had been freed from a rule or
ritual-oriented religious life. Their relationship with God is not precariously dependent on performing certain
tasks or avoiding certain religious taboos. The other group was also a fully Christian, and a fully accepted,
and a fully committed group of believers. However, they viewed their faith through the religious ideas of
their past experiences. The Jewish believers tended to hold on to the Old Covenant practices of Judaism. The
converted pagans tended to retain some of their old religious (pagan) ideas and practices. But notice that
Paul did not call this mindset among believers "sin." It is only when they violated their consciences that it
became sin (cf. Rom. 14:23).

The term adunatos, "without strength" (cf. Acts 14:8) is connected to the term
astheneō (cf. Rom. 14:1,21; 1 Cor. 8:7,10,11,12; 9:22), which also means "without strength."

This text implies that Christians should not grudgingly tolerate other Christians, but should
lovingly "care for" and "work with" them.

The term, "bear" was also used of Jesus' "cross bearing" in
John 19:17 and Luke 14:27. Paul knew the tensions that can occur between religious people. He was trained
under Gamaliel, who was a rabbi of the liberal rabbinical school of Hillel. Remember, Paul wrote Romans from Corinth!

▣ "and not just please ourselves" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE with
the NEGATIVE PARTICLE, which usually means stop an act in process. Self-centeredness is a sure
sign of immaturity; following Christ's example (cf. Rom. 15:3; Phil. 2:1-11) is the sign of maturity. Again,
it is "the strong" who were being addressed (cf. Rom. 14:1,14,16,21,27). This is not to imply they had all the
responsibility in maintaining the fellowship. "The weak" are also addressed in Rom. 14:3, 20, 23; 15:5-6,7.

15:2 "Each of us is to please his neighbor" This is "neighbor" used in the sense of fellow Christian.
This does not imply personal compromise of convictions, but that one does not push his personal preferences
or opinions in the ambiguous areas. The unity and growth of the body of Christ, not personal freedom, is
paramount (cf. 1 Cor. 9:19-23; 10:24-33; Eph. 4:1-16)!!!

▣

NASB
"for his edification"

NKJV
"leading to edification"

NRSV
"for the good purpose of building up the neighbor"

TEV
"in order to build them up in the faith"

NJB
"help them to become stronger Christians"

REB
"and will build up the common life"

Peshitta
"in good and constructive ways"

This is the major theme of Romans 14 (cf. Rom. 14:16,19). It is also one of the tests for
spiritual gifts found in 1 Cor. 10:23; 12:7; 14:26; Eph. 4:29.

In this context it refers to "the strong" believer limiting his/her freedom in love for the
purpose of helping fellow Christians grow in faith. Joseph A. Fitzmyer and Raymond E. Brown, ed., The
Jerome Biblical Commentary, vol. 2, has an interesting comment on this verse.

"This phrase is often taken to mean 'to edify him' (the neighbor), referring to the personal
development of one's Christian neighbor. But considering that Paul often uses the building metaphor in his
letters in a corporate sense, the phrase undoubtedly has a social, corporate meaning, here as well (cf.
1 Cor. 14:12; Eph. 4:12; Rom. 14:19)" (p. 328).

It must be restated that this context is not implying that "weak" brothers should become "strong" brothers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDIFY

15:3 "For even Christ" Christ is our pattern and example. This truth is also stressed in Rom. 15:5;
Phil. 2:1-11; 1 Pet. 2:21; 1 John 3:16.

Jesus was incarnate to accomplish three spiritual tasks.

- to give His life as a substitute for human sin

- to fully, completely, and ultimately reveal the character and purpose of YHWH

- to give redeemed humans an example to follow

▣ "it is written" This is a PRESENT PASSIVE INDICATIVE, which is a Hebrew idiom
for Scripture. This is a quote from Psalm 69:9. By referring to Christ's example (did not please Himself, cf. Phil. 2:5-8)
in addition to an OT quote, Paul uses the two most important sources of authority in the early church (cf. Newman and Nida,
A Translator's Handbook on Paul's Letter to the Romans, p. 271). The selflessness of Christ as He bore the sin of
all the world is our example (cf. 1 John 3:16).

Paul seems to link

- Jesus' bearing reproach as the Messiah

- Paul bearing the reproach of the gospel

There is a price to pay for serving God in a fallen world.

- the rejected and crucified Jesus

- Paul tells of his rejection and persecution in 2 Cor. 4:7-12; 6:3-10; 11:23-33. Paul was
finally beheaded in Rome

15:4 "for whatever was written in earlier times was written for our instruction" The OT was

- written for the education and guidance of NT believers also (cf. Rom. 4:23-24; 15:4; 1 Cor. 9:10; 10:6,11).

- It is relevant to new covenant believers (cf. 2 Tim. 2:15; 3:16-17).

- There is a continuity, but also a discontinuity between the Old and New Testaments.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEWS OF THE MOSAIC LAW

▣ "so that through perseverance and the encouragement of the Scriptures" Notice how the truth of
God's Word and believers' lifestyle response to it are combined. Faith and practice are bound together (cf.
Rom. 15:5). They result in confidence in life, in death, and at the promised hope of Christ's return.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSEVERANCE

▣ "we might have hope" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE SUBJUNCTIVE, which implies our
hope is dependant on the actions mentioned earlier in Rom. 15:4. In the NT "hope" often referred to some eschatological
event when our salvation will be consummated (cf. Rom. 8:30; 1 John 3:2). This Greek term does not
have the connotation of uncertainty as the English term. The Second Coming is a certain event with an
uncertain time element.

Paul uses this term often in several different but related senses. Often it is associated with
the consummation of the believer's faith. This can be expressed as glory, eternal life, ultimate salvation,
Second Coming, etc. The consummation is certain but the time element is future and unknown. It is often
associated with "faith" and "love" (cf. 1 Cor. 13:13; 1 Thess. 1:3; 2 Thess. 2:16). A partial list of some of
Paul's uses are:

- The Second Coming, Gal. 5:5; Eph. 1:18; 4:4; Titus 2:13

- Jesus is our hope, 1 Tim. 1:1

- Trust in the gospel, Col. 1:23

- Ultimate salvation, Col. 1:5; 1 Thess. 4:13; 5:8

- The glory of God, Rom. 5:2, 2 Cor. 3:12; Col. 1:27

- Assurance of salvation, 1 Thess. 5:8

- Eternal life, Titus 1:2; 3:7

- Redemption of all creation, Rom. 8:20

- Faith, Rom. 8:23-25, 15:4

- Title of God, Rom. 15:13

- Paul's desire for believers, 2 Cor. 1:7

15:5 "may the God. . .grant" This is a rare AORIST ACTIVE OPTATIVE, which expresses a
wish or prayer. Paul's prayer, Rom. 15:5-6, had two petitions.

- to be in one mind (cf. Rom. 12:16; 2 Cor. 13:11; Phil. 2:2)

- to be in one voice of praise to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (cf. Rom. 15:6, 7,9)

▣ "the God who gives perseverance and encouragement" This is almost a descriptive title of God
(cf. Rom. 15:13; 1 Cor. 1:3). These characteristics of God come to believers through the Scriptures (cf.
Rom. 15:4).

These descriptive titles for God are so meaningful that I wanted to give you some other examples
that come to my mind.

- "to Him who is able" ‒ Rom. 16:25; Eph. 3:20; Jude v. 24

- "the God of hope" ‒ Rom. 1:13

- "God of peace" ‒ Rom. 15:33; 16:20; Phil. 4:9; Heb. 13:20

- "the only wise God" ‒ Rom. 16:27

- "the Father of mercies" ‒ 2 Cor. 1:3

- "God of all comfort" ‒ 2 Cor. 1:3

- "God of love and peace" ‒ 2 Cor. 13:11

- "the Father of glory" ‒ Eph. 1:17

- "the Majesty on high" ‒ Heb. 1:5; also note 2 Pet. 1:17

- "the Father of Lightds" ‒ James 1:17

Wow, what a God we trust and serve!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE NEED TO PERSEVERE

15:6 "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" This is Deity's full NT title (cf. 2 Cor. 1:3;
Eph. 1:3; Col. 1:3; 1 Pet. 1:3; notice a similar title in Rom. 1:7). This is not the God of philosophical
necessity, but of revelation. Notice the two titles of God in Paul's prayer of Rom. 15:5-6.

- the God of perseverance and encouragement

- the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FATHERHOOD OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRIST JESUS AS LORD

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ROMANS 15:7-13

7Therefore, accept one another, just as Christ also accepted
us to the glory of God. 8For I say that Christ has become a servant to the circumcision on behalf of
the truth of God to confirm the promises given to the fathers, 9and for the Gentiles to glorify
God for His mercy; as it is written,

"Therefore I will give praise to You among the Gentiles,

And I will sing to Your name."

10Again he says,

"Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people."

11And again,

"Praise the Lord all you Gentiles,

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- What is the central truth of Romans 14:1-15:13?

- Why does Paul quote the OT passages in verses 9-12? What great truth do they teach?

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ROMANS 15:14-33

- In many ways the close of this letter is similar to its opening, Rom. 1:8-15

- it extols their faith (cf. Rom. 1:8)

- it defends Paul's apostleship of the gospel to the Gentiles (cf. Rom. 1:13,14)

- it asserts Paul's desire to visit them (cf. Rom. 1:10,13)

- it expresses Paul's desire that they would help him on his way to other regions not yet
evangelized (i.e., Spain, cf. Rom. 1:13)

- Again, there is a hint of the tension in the Roman Church between believing Jews and believing
Gentiles which has been alluded to or hinted at throughout the letter, but especially Romans 9-11;
14:1-15:13. Remember, the NT letters are like listening to one half of a phone conversation. The other
side must be understood from

- the intention of the original author

- the historical setting of those who received the letters

- Also there is a hint of the tension in the early church concerning Paul's apostolic standing. He
seems to defend himself in Rom. 15:15-19; 1:2,5.

- This literary unit contains two topics.

- Paul's apostolic, evangelistic, Gentile-oriented ministry (cf. Rom. 15:14-21)

- Paul's travel plans to accomplish this purpose may take him through Rome (cf. Rom. 15:22-33)

The "I" (auto egō) is very emphatic in Greek. Paul is truly complimenting this

Paul asserts three things about these Roman Christians in Rom. 15:14.

- they are full of goodness (PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE)

- they are full of knowledge (PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE)

- they are able to admonish one another (PRESENT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE)

This verse implies that Paul is not bringing a new message to them, but explaining and clarifying
the good news which they already had heard and accepted (cf. Rom. 15:15). No one knows who started the church
in Rome. It was not Peter. Most commentators suppose it was those Jews visiting Jerusalem for Pentecost who heard
Peter preach and trusted Christ. As they went home to their synagogue, they brought the gospel with them.

▣ "you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all" As the "I myself" is emphatic in the
first phrase, "you yourselves" is emphatic here. The term "full" (mestos) means "full of" or "replete."
Paul used this term only twice, both times in Romans (Rom. 1:29; 15:14).

The term "filled" (plēroō) is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE.
Paul used this term often in Romans (cf. Rom. 1:29; 8:4; 13:8; 15:13,14,19). He also uses the
NOUN plērōma often in Romans (cf. Rom. 11:12,25; 13:10; 15:29), but never the
ADJECTIVE in any of his writings.

It was Paul's desire that a full gospel completely fill believers to overflow in love and
service. Believers have all they need in Christ. They need to fully accept and receive this assurance.

A Textual Commentary on the Greek NT.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- How is the OT a benefit to NT believers (Rom. 15:4-5; 1 Cor. 10:6,11)?

- Why does Paul quote the OT in Rom. 15:9-12? What great truth do they teach?

- Where in this section of Romans does the tension between Jew and Gentile possibly appear?

- Where in this section of Romans does the tension about Paul's apostleship appear?

- What was Paul's reason for the offering of the Gentile churches for the church in Jerusalem
(Rom. 15:15-28)?

- What was Paul's missionary strategy? Why did he want to go to Spain?

- How and why does Paul describe his work as that of a priest (v.16) relating to Israel as a
Kingdom of Priests (Exod. 19:5-6) or to the church (I. Pet. 2: 5,9; Rev. 1:6)?

- Did God answer Paul's prayer of verses 30-33?
